---
title: "Packages, algorithms and help"
subtitle: "Which tool for which task - and what is available on DST"
date: last-modified
---

This is a reference hub: which tool solves which task, whether it is available
on DST, and where to find more help. The guide takes you to an analysis-ready
dataset and points you towards the right tools for the actual analysis - but
does **not teach the statistical methods**. For that you need a statistician, a
course, or the packages' own documentation.

## 1. Validated algorithms

Published, peer-reviewed methods you can use directly to construct covariates.
SEPLINE is a guideline rather than a package: worked, not yet validated code
for it is on [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd).

::: {.wide-first-col}
  | Algorithm                                                                                           | What it does                                              | Use it to                                                                     | Article                                                          |
  | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | **[Open Source Diabetes Classifier (OSDC)](osdc.qmd)**                                              | Classifies everyone in Denmark as T1D, T2D or no diabetes | Define a diabetes population, type and inclusion date                         | [doi:10.2147/CLEP.S407019](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S407019) |
  | **[Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI)](nmi.qmd)**                                                    | Weighted mortality-risk score (50 predictors)             | Adjust for mortality risk / predict 5-year mortality (NOT comorbidity burden) | [doi:10.2147/CLEP.S353398](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S353398) |
  | **[SEPLINE - Socioeconomic Position in Epidemiological Research](socioeconomic-variables.qmd)** | National guideline for socioeconomic variables            | Education, income, employment as covariates                                   | [doi:10.2147/CLEP.S520772](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772) |
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Charlson for comorbidity burden (not NMI):** both `heaven::charlsonIndex()`
and `EpiForsk` (see below) calculate Charlson comorbidity score from LPR
diagnoses - both are on DST.
:::

## 2. Existing functions for data management and extraction

### `heaven` - Danish register data toolkit

*(pre-installed on DST; not on CRAN -
[github.com/tagteam/heaven](https://github.com/tagteam/heaven))*

Functions built specifically for Danish register data by Thomas Gerds
(University of Copenhagen, Biostatistics): Lexis-splitting for time-varying
covariates, drug exposure windows from LMDB, risk-set matching, Charlson score,
average income, hypertension from prescriptions, and built-in lookup tables for
education and ATC codes.

<details>
<summary>What heaven can do - and when to use it</summary>

**Lexis-splitting** - split follow-up time across multiple time axes when a covariate changes over time (age, calendar period, time since exposure).

```r
library(heaven)

# Age bands: the split points are added to each person's birth date
df_split <- lexisSeq(
  indat       = cohort,
  invars      = c("pnr", "inn", "out", "event"),   # id, start date, end date, outcome (0/1) - in that order
  varname     = "birth_date",                       # date the split points are added to
  splitvector = round(c(40, 50, 60, 70) * 365.25),  # age boundaries, in days
  format      = "vector",
  value       = "age_band"                          # 0 before age 40, then +1 at each boundary
)
# Calendar periods: fixed dates, nothing added (varname = NULL)
df_split <- lexisSeq(
  indat       = df_split,
  invars      = c("pnr", "inn", "out", "event"),
  splitvector = as.Date(c("2010-01-01", "2015-01-01", "2020-01-01")),
  format      = "vector",
  value       = "period"
)
# Returns: a data.table with MORE rows per person - one per time interval.
# The new columns (age_band, period) count how many split points have passed.
# Ready for a Cox model with time-varying covariates. To split on event dates
# (e.g. comorbidity onset) instead, use lexisTwo().
```

**Drug exposure from LMDB** - calculate exposure periods from prescription data (e.g. "was the person on metformin at index date?").

```r
# One list per drug: the ATC codes, and per pack strength (value) the assumed
# minimum, maximum and default daily dose - the numbers here are illustrative.
metformin <- list(
  atc      = "A10BA02",
  maxdepot = 4000,                                # max total dose a person can stockpile
  period   = as.Date(c("1995-01-01", "2024-12-31")),
  prescriptionwindow = 2,
  doses    = list(value = c(500, 850, 1000),     # strengths (strnum) in your data
                  min   = c(500, 850, 1000),
                  max   = c(3000, 3000, 3000),
                  def   = c(1000, 1700, 2000))
)
exp_table <- medicinMacro(
  drugs  = list(metformin = metformin),
  drugdb = lmdb_data,  # pnr, eksd, atc, strnum, packsize, apk
  admdb  = NULL        # or admissions from getAdmLimits() to pause exposure during stays
)
# Returns: a list with one data.table per drug (exp_table$metformin): one row
# per exposure period per person, with firstday, lastday and the estimated
# daily dose. Use subsequent joins to determine exposure at index date.
```

**Charlson comorbidity score** from LPR diagnoses:

```r
charlson_data <- charlsonIndex(data = lpr_diag_data, ptid = "pnr",
                               vars = "c_diag",              # D-prefixed codes, as in LPR
                               data.date = "d_inddto",       # date of each diagnosis
                               charlson.date = "index_date", # date the index is computed at
                               look.back = 5)                # years
# Returns: a list of two data.tables - [[1]] the Charlson index per (pnr,
# index_date), [[2]] binary indicators per Charlson disease group. People with
# no Charlson diagnosis are missing from both: set them to 0 after joining.
```

**Risk-set matching** - match cases to controls at index date (`incidenceMatch()`; `exposureMatch()` when exposure defines the case):

```r
matched <- incidenceMatch(ptid = "pnr", event = "event",    # event: 0/1
                          terms = c("koen", "birth_year"),   # exact matching - character/factor
                          data = cohort, n.controls = 5,
                          case.index = "event_date",         # NA for non-cases
                          end.followup = "end_date")         # death, emigration, study end
# Returns: data.table of cases and their selected controls, with case.id
# linking each case to its controls.
```

**Average income over the years before a date** - what [Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income) does by hand:

```r
income <- averageIncome(
  data       = cohort,                          # id + the date to look back from
  income     = faik_linked,                     # id + year + income, already linked to pnr
  datvars    = c("pnr", "index_date"),
  incomevars = c("pnr", "year", "famaekvivadisp_13"),
  numyears   = 3                                # default is 5; SEPLINE uses 3
)
# Returns: one row per person with the averaged income.
# It uses only years STRICTLY BEFORE the index year, and it keeps one row per
# person-year, so repeated rows for the same person and year collapse.
# It does NOT build the familie_id bridge for you - the income table you pass in
# must already be linked to pnr.
```

**Hypertension from prescriptions** - `hypertensionMedication(data, vars, index.date, medication.definition = hypertensionATC)`. Defines hypertension from ATC codes, either at a given index date or across the whole period. Arguments are not self-explanatory - run `help(hypertensionMedication)` before using it.

**Find records by partial code match** - `findCondition(data, vars, keep, conditions, exclusions, match = "contain")`. The packaged version of "keep the rows whose code starts with one of these" - the pattern used throughout [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd). Run `help(findCondition)` for the argument order.

**Municipality to region** - `kommuneRegion(kommune)` converts a numeric 3-digit municipality code to one of the five regions. Valid from 2007. Input must be numeric, not character.

**Built-in lookup tables** - two of them replace hand-written code lists:

```r
data(edu_code)  # 4,621 rows: hfaudd -> education category
# Columns: hfaudd, edu_uk / edu_dk (15 categories), code5 / code5txt (5 levels),
# isced / isced_code (ISCED 0-9). Join it on hfaudd instead of writing your own
# case_when() over the digits of hfaudd, which does not give the level -
# see socioeconomic-variables.qmd and register-reference.qmd (UDDA).

data(hypertensionATC)  # ATC codes per class of antihypertensive drug
```

::: {.callout-note}
`heaven` is confirmed available on DST - use `library(heaven)` directly. It is not on CRAN, so outside DST it must be fetched from [GitHub](https://github.com/tagteam/heaven). Function documentation lives in the package itself (`help(name)`); the maintainers also keep a worked walkthrough at [examples/user-heaven.org](https://github.com/tagteam/heaven/blob/master/examples/user-heaven.org).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**`heaven` is built with a different package than the rest of this guide.**

This guide uses `dplyr` (part of the tidyverse) for handling tables. `heaven` is
written with `data.table`, which is another package that does the same job in a
different style. That means the tables `heaven` hands back are `data.table`
tables rather than the ones you are used to.

**You do not need to learn `data.table` to use `heaven`.** A `data.table` is
still an ordinary table, so `filter()`, `mutate()`, `select()` and
`left_join()` all work on it exactly as before. The only thing you will notice
is that it looks a little different when you print it in the console: it numbers
the rows and shows the column types differently.

If you want to be completely sure you are back on familiar ground, convert the
result once with `as_tibble()` and carry on:

```r
income <- averageIncome(...) %>% as_tibble()
```
:::

</details>

### `EpiForsk` - register data helper functions from SSI

*(CRAN; on DST -
[github.com/Laksafoss/EpiForsk](https://github.com/Laksafoss/EpiForsk))*

Code-sharing package from the Statens Serum Institut. Particularly useful:
`flatten_date_intervals()` which merges overlapping hospital contacts into
continuous periods - necessary before comorbidity lookback. Danish Charlson
score included.

<details>
<summary>Most important functions and when to use them</summary>

**`flatten_date_intervals()` - overlapping contacts**

A person can have two overlapping admissions in LPR (e.g. a transfer). Before comorbidity lookback, overlapping periods must be merged:

```r
library(EpiForsk)

lpr_flat <- flatten_date_intervals(
  data = lpr_contacts, id = pnr,        # bare column names, no quotes
  in_date = d_inddto, out_date = d_uddto
)
# Returns: a data frame with merged start/end per person -
# overlapping periods are reduced to the total covered period.
```

**`charlson_score()` - Danish-calibrated Charlson comorbidity score** from ICD-10 (incl. D-prefix). See the callout below for what it requires.

```r
charlson <- charlson_score(data = lpr_diag_data, Person_ID = pnr, diagnosis_variable = c_diag)
# Returns: one row per person with three Charlson variants
# (CCI_Quan, CCI_Christiensen, CCI_Charlson_Deyo).
```

::: {.callout-important}
**What does `charlson_score()` require?**
You must extract a lookback period from LPR yourself (typically 5 years before index date) and give the function **all diagnoses** in that window - all diagnosis types. You do **not** need to filter on specific ICD codes in advance; the function matches the codes to Charlson categories itself. The D-prefix (`DG30` etc.) is handled by EpiForsk - it does not need to be stripped first.

```r
# Example: extract lookback and pass all diagnoses
# pnr and d_inddto are in lpr_adm - not lpr_diag

# One row per (pnr, index_date), with each person's own 5-year lookback
# window already attached - this table is the size of your cohort, not the
# register. If your cohort has repeated pnr (e.g. matched with replacement),
# each occurrence gets its own row and its own window here.
lookback_keys <- cohort %>%
  mutate(window_start = index_date - 365.25 * 5,
         window_end   = index_date - 1)

lpr2_lookback <- lpr_adm %>%
  select(pnr, recnum, d_inddto) %>%
  # Coarse filter first (cheap): narrow to the union of every window in the
  # cohort, before the join - !! injects a single computed value, not a column
  filter(d_inddto >= !!min(lookback_keys$window_start)) %>%
  # copy = TRUE sends the small lookback_keys table into the database, so the
  # join runs there, not in R. This matters more here than almost anywhere
  # else in the guide: Charlson needs EVERY A/B/G diagnosis in the window,
  # not a filtered-down code list, so the unjoined, unwindowed data for a
  # whole cohort can be large. Collecting it all into R FIRST and only then
  # joining to cohort/filtering by index_date (the previous version of this
  # example did exactly that) has been known to pull tens of GB into RAM and
  # crash the R session - the same failure mode documented for NMI's LMDB
  # extraction, see nmi.qmd, fixed the same way.
  inner_join(lookback_keys, by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  # Precise filter (correctness): each row against its OWN window, not the global one
  filter(d_inddto >= window_start, d_inddto < index_date) %>%
  inner_join(
    lpr_diag %>%
      filter(c_diagtype %in% c("A", "B", "G")) %>%   # A/B/G for comorbidity - Charlson needs all of them, no ICD filter
      select(recnum, c_diag),
    by = "recnum"
  ) %>%
  select(pnr, index_date, d_inddto, c_diag) %>%
  collect()

charlson <- charlson_score(data = lpr2_lookback, Person_ID = pnr, diagnosis_variable = c_diag)
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**`Person_ID = pnr` alone is not enough if your cohort has repeated `pnr`.**
`lpr2_lookback` above is correctly windowed per `(pnr, index_date)`, but
`charlson_score()` itself only groups by the single `Person_ID` column you give it -
it has no way to know about `index_date`. For a comparison cohort matched
**with replacement**, that means diagnoses from *all* of a person's
`index_date` windows get pooled into one Charlson score, silently reattached
to every occurrence of their `pnr`. If this applies to you, build a single
combined key first (e.g. `mutate(pnr_index = paste(pnr, index_date))`) and
pass `Person_ID = pnr_index` instead, then split the two columns back apart from
the result afterwards.
:::

</details>

### `dataReporter` - automatic data quality report {#datareporter-automatic-data-quality-report}

*(CRAN; confirmed on DST -
[github.com/ekstroem/dataReporter](https://github.com/ekstroem/dataReporter))*

Automatically generates an HTML/PDF report of all columns in a dataset:
distribution, missing values, outliers and type checks. Useful for validating a
new register extraction before starting analysis. Published in Journal of
Statistical Software.

```r
library(dataReporter)
makeDataReport(my_extract) # opens report in browser
```

See also [Phase 7 - Inspect your data](inspect-data.qmd) for manual
inspection commands.

### `fiktive` - synthetic Danish register data

*(GitHub only - local use only -
[github.com/sara-schwartz/fiktive](https://github.com/sara-schwartz/fiktive))*

Fictitious register tables for practising and testing code locally *without*
DST access. Not used on the server. Install with
`remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive")`.

What it generates is the **Available registers** table in the package README,
not the whole registers-guide schema. That table
currently covers population (`bef`, quarterly), labour classification (`akm`),
cancer, deaths and cause of death (`dod`, `dodsaars`, `dodsaasg`,
`dodsaarsager`), family income (`faik`), laboratory results (`lab_dm_forsker`,
`labka`), prescriptions (`lmdb`), LPR2 somatic contacts and their child tables,
LPR3 contacts, diagnoses, and procedures, psychiatric LPR (`t_psyk_*`), live
births (`mfr`), primary-care settlements (`sysi`, `sssy`), education (`udda`),
and migrations (`vnds`, `vnds_hist`, `vnds_ind`, `vnds_ud`), plus the bundled
cohort tables `dch` and `dchng`. A child table has to be in the same
`generate_registers()` call as its parent. See [Phase 6 - First
extraction](first-extraction.qmd).

### `fastreg` - SAS → parquet (and reading registers back)

*(CRAN; `install.packages("fastreg")` -
[dp-next.github.io/fastreg](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/))*

The recommended tool for converting SAS registers to parquet. It **converts**
(`convert()`, partitioned by year, with a `use_template()` targets pipeline for
the whole workspace) and **reads back** (`read_register("bef")` returns a lazy
DuckDB connection, reading all yearly subfolders as one dataset). Set
`options(fastreg.project_rawdata_dir=, fastreg.project_workdata_dir=)` once,
then refer to registers by name. See [Parquet and fastreg - SAS →
parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet).

`read_register()` only finds registers in fastreg's own format
(`<register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet`). For any other parquet the package has
`list_parquet_datasets()`, `read_parquet_dataset()` and `read_parquet_file()` -
see [When `read_register()` cannot find the
register](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#when-read-register-fails).

## 3. Analysis tools

All packages in this section are **confirmed on DST** (June 2026). The guide
does not teach the statistical methods - see package documentation for
methodological choices.

### `survival` - the foundation for survival analysis

*(CRAN; always available -
[cran.r-project.org/package=survival](https://cran.r-project.org/package=survival))*

Provides `Surv(time, status)`, `coxph()` and `survfit()` - the fundamental
building blocks on which all survival packages below are built. You rarely call
`{survival}` directly for plots and tables, but `library(survival)` belongs at
the top of your analysis scripts.

```r
library(survival)
cox <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age + sex + nmi, data = cohort)
summary(cox) # HR, 95% CI, p-values - pass to Publish or gtsummary for formatted output
```

### `gtsummary` - Table 1 and manuscript tables

*(CRAN -
[cran.r-project.org/package=gtsummary](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gtsummary))*

Standard for manuscript tables: `tbl_summary()` for Table 1 stratified by
exposure, `tbl_regression()` for Cox and logistic regression, `tbl_survfit()`
for survival summaries. Published in R Journal 2021.

<details>
<summary>Example: Table 1</summary>

```r
library(gtsummary)

table1 <- cohort %>%
  select(group, age, sex, nmi, occupation_cat) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = group,                                                # stratify by exposure
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous()  ~ "{mean} ({sd})",                    # continuous: mean (SD)
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"                        # categorical: n (%)
    ),
    missing = "no"
  ) %>%
  add_overall() %>%
  add_p()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Output control:** counts below DST's threshold (fewer than 5) must not be exported, and a suppressed cell must not be recoverable from totals or other cells. Rounding alone does not achieve this - see [Export and repatriation](export.qmd) for the rules. [`Z.gtsummary.addons::round_5_gtsummary()`](https://github.com/zheer-kejlberg/Z.gtsummary.addons) shows counts of 0-4 as "<5" and rounds the rest to the nearest 5 - not on DST, import via data manager.
:::

</details>

### `carpenter` - pipe-based table structure

*(CRAN -
[github.com/lwjohnst86/carpenter](https://github.com/lwjohnst86/carpenter))*

Older alternative to `gtsummary` with a simpler pipe-based API: start with
`outline_table()`, add rows with `add_rows()`, finish with `build_table()`. By
Luke Johnston.

```r
library(carpenter)

outline_table(cohort, "group") %>%
  add_rows("age", stat_meanSD) %>% # continuous: mean (SD)
  add_rows("sex", stat_nPct) %>% # categorical: n (%)
  add_rows("nmi", stat_medianIQR) %>% # continuous: median (IQR)
  build_table()
```

### `prodlim` - Kaplan--Meier and Aalen--Johansen cumulative incidence

*(CRAN - [github.com/tagteam/prodlim](https://github.com/tagteam/prodlim))*

Estimates and plots survival curves and cumulative incidence. `Hist()` handles
competing risks with a single status variable: 0 = censored, 1 = primary event,
2 = competing event (e.g. death). Use `prodlim` for descriptive curves -
`riskRegression` for regression.

<details>
<summary>Example: KM curve and Aalen–Johansen</summary>

```r
library(prodlim)

# Kaplan–Meier:
fit_km <- prodlim(Hist(time, event) ~ group, data = cohort)
plot(fit_km)

# Aalen–Johansen cumulative incidence (competing risks):
# status: 0 = censored, 1 = primary event, 2 = competing event (e.g. death)
fit_aj <- prodlim(Hist(time, status) ~ group, data = cohort)
plot(fit_aj, cause = 1)   # cumulative incidence for primary event
```

::: {.callout-note}
KM alone **overestimates** cumulative incidence in the presence of competing risks. Use Aalen–Johansen (`cause = 1`) instead.
:::

</details>

### `riskRegression` - Cause-Specific Cox, Fine-Gray and absolute risk

*(CRAN -
[github.com/tagteam/riskRegression](https://github.com/tagteam/riskRegression))*

For regression with competing risks. `CSC()` fits Cause-Specific Cox (one model
per cause), `FGR()` fits Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard. `predictRisk()`
computes absolute risk at specific time points. `Score()` validates and compares
models (Brier score, time-dependent AUC).

<details>
<summary>Example: CSC model and absolute risk</summary>

```r
library(riskRegression)
library(survival)

# Cause-Specific Cox:
csc_model <- CSC(Hist(time, status) ~ age + sex + nmi, data = cohort)
summary(csc_model)

# Absolute risk at 1, 3 and 5 years for primary event:
ar <- predictRisk(csc_model, newdata = cohort,
                  times = c(1, 3, 5), cause = 1)
# ar: matrix - one column per time point, one row per person
```

</details>

### `Publish` - regression results ready for manuscript

*(CRAN - [github.com/tagteam/Publish](https://github.com/tagteam/Publish))*

`regressionTable()` takes a fitted model (Cox, logistic, linear) and returns a
table with estimates, 95% CI and p-values. `plotConfidence()` produces forest
plots from the same output.

```r
library(Publish)
library(survival)

cox_model <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age + sex + nmi, data = cohort)

regressionTable(cox_model) # HR, 95% CI, p-values
plot(regressionTable(cox_model)) # forest plot (calls plotConfidence())
```

### `MatchIt` - propensity score and exact matching

*(CRAN -
[cran.r-project.org/package=MatchIt](https://cran.r-project.org/package=MatchIt))*

Matches exposed to unexposed on observed covariates. Supports nearest-neighbour,
exact and optimal matching. `summary()` gives balance statistics (SMD),
`match.data()` returns the matched dataset. Alternative to
`heaven::incidenceMatch()` with better balance diagnostics.

<details>
<summary>Example: 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching</summary>

```r
library(MatchIt)

m <- matchit(exposed ~ age + sex + nmi,
             data   = cohort,
             method = "nearest",   # nearest-neighbour matching
             ratio  = 1)           # 1:1

# Balance check - SMD < 0.1 is a common rule of thumb:
summary(m, standardize = TRUE)

# Matched dataset:
matched <- match.data(m)
```

</details>

### `pec` - prediction error curves

*(CRAN -
[cran.r-project.org/package=pec](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pec))*

Computes and plots Brier score over time for comparing and validating prediction
models. Niche - only relevant for prediction models; `riskRegression::Score()`
usually covers the need.

### `BuyseTest` - Generalised Pairwise Comparisons

*(CRAN, confirmed on DST v3.3.3 -
[github.com/bozenne/BuyseTest](https://github.com/bozenne/BuyseTest))*

Implements Generalised Pairwise Comparisons (GPC): compares two groups via win
ratio, net benefit and win probability on **prioritised endpoints**. Niche -
relevant when you have a hierarchy of endpoints and want to avoid classical
event-time assumptions.

```r
library(BuyseTest)

# One time-to-event endpoint:
result <- BuyseTest(
  group ~ tte(time, event, threshold = 0),
  data = cohort,
  method.inference = "u-statistic"
)
summary(result) # win ratio, net benefit, win probability
```

`powerBuyseTest()` calculates the required sample size given desired power and
expected effect - useful before data collection or grant applications.

### `kinship2` - pedigrees and kinship matrices

*(CRAN -
[cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kinship2](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kinship2/index.html))*

Creates pedigree objects from parent--child relationships and computes kinship
coefficients (probability that alleles drawn at random from the two people are
identical by descent: 0.25 for parent/child and for full siblings). Useful for multi-generational family studies. By Terry Therneau (Mayo
Clinic).

<details>
<summary>Example: create pedigree and compute kinship</summary>

```r
library(kinship2)

# Create pedigree:
# DST's koen variable (1 = male, 2 = female) matches kinship2's expectation directly
ped <- pedigree(
  id    = family$pnr,
  dadid = family$pnr_father,   # NA if father unknown
  momid = family$pnr_mother,   # NA if mother unknown
  sex   = family$koen           # 1 = male, 2 = female
)

# Kinship coefficients:
km <- kinship(ped)

# Visualise family tree:
plot(ped)
```

</details>

### `tame` - cluster medication exposure from LMDB

*(CRAN - [github.com/Laksafoss/tame](https://github.com/Laksafoss/tame))*

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering of medication data using a custom distance
measure combining ATC classification, timing and dose. `medic()` is the primary
function. Relevant for characterising polypharmacy patterns in cohorts. By
Anders Laksafoss (SSI).

<details>
<summary>Example: cluster medication patterns</summary>

```r
library(tame)

# Cluster on ATC code alone:
clust <- medic(lmdb_data, id = pnr, atc = atc, k = 5)
# k = desired number of clusters - choose with scree plot or domain knowledge

# With timing information (column range):
clust <- medic(lmdb_data, id = pnr, atc = atc,
               timing = trimester_1:trimester_3,   # columns defining time windows
               k = 5)

summary(clust)   # summarise clusters
```

::: {.callout-note}
`id`, `atc` and `timing` use bare column names (NSE - no quotes). `lmdb_data` must have one row per prescription dispensing.
:::

</details>

### Possible inspiration - not confirmed on DST

**[`famnet`](https://github.com/lwjohnst86/famnet)** *(GitHub, experimental)* -
identifies family relationships from person IDs: given a dataset with PersonID,
FatherID and MotherID, `fmn_siblings()` finds all sibling pairs with
relationship type. Relevant for family linkage across generations in Danish
register data. By Luke Johnston.

**[`plotsurv`](https://github.com/zheer-kejlberg/plotsurv)** *(GitHub, not on
DST)* - publication-ready Kaplan--Meier and Aalen--Johansen competing-risks
plots with at-risk table, CI bands and censoring ticks.
`plotsurv(survfit_object)`.

**[`Z.gtsummary.addons`](https://github.com/zheer-kejlberg/Z.gtsummary.addons)**
*(GitHub, not on DST)* - extends `gtsummary` with `add_SMD()` (standardised mean
differences for Table 1) and `round_5_gtsummary()` (rounds counts to the nearest
5 - relevant for DST output control).
